item.title: TimeArch: A Multi-Agent Approach for Software Architecture Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.06921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI is making software implementation faster, but not necessarily better architected. Most current GenAI coding workflows move directly from prompts to code, while the architectural reasoning that should connect requirements, quality attributes, stakeholders, design decisions, and implementation remains weakly supported. Architectural styles, system decomposition, tradeoff analysis, quality-attribute decisions, and stakeholder concerns are often left implicit or handled outside the AI-supported workflow. This creates a missing architectural layer between requirements and code, limiting traceability, validation, and governance in GenAI-enabled software development. This paper presents TimeArch, a multi-agent approach that makes this architectural layer explicit. TimeArch structures software architecture design as a governed lifecycle rather than a one-shot generation task. It combines agent-based reasoning with retrieval-augmented grounding to support requirement definition, architecture design, validation and assurance, and delivery and evolution. The approach supports requirement capture, architectural driver identification, design reasoning, validation, and decision documentation within a traceable process. We demonstrate TimeArch through a working prototype that operationalizes the proposed approach and assess its feasibility using representative software architecture design cases from multiple domains with heterogeneous inputs. As future work, we plan to conduct comprehensive industrial case studies to evaluate the adoption and use of TimeArch in both new and existing software projects. A TimeArch demo is available at: https://sda-assistant.com/. Keywords: AI-native software architecture; requirements-driven software architecture; architectural reasoning; architecture traceability; architecture validation

item.title: Towards Comprehensive Mobile Application Testing for User-centric Feature Coverage via Simulating Real-World Users with Personas
item.description: arXiv:2611.06922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for black-box mobile application testing, where the ultimate goal is the comprehensive coverage of the features users rely on. However, most existing studies focus on Activity Coverage, which measures the proportion of distinct application screens visited during a test session but does not directly measure whether agents actually test the features users care about. To address this, we focus on (1) how to automatically measure whether a testing framework covers the features users care about, and (2) how to design a framework that achieves more comprehensive feature coverage. To answer (1), we introduce the User-Centric Feature Coverage benchmark, which consists of two components: a manually crafted dataset of 3,012 user-centric target features based on real reviews and app descriptions, and an automated evaluation pipeline that translates agent-generated test cases and target features into a shared semantic space, then uses an LLM-as-a-judge to compute coverage. To answer (2), we introduce ECS (Exploration, Critical User Journeys, and Synthetic Reviews). ECS is a framework that explores the application, then uses an LLM to convert exploration traces into Critical User Journeys (CUJs) to bring the semantic meaning of the trace closer to a distinct feature. Each CUJ consists of an LLM-inferred user intent paired with reproducible test steps. ECS then aggregates multiple CUJs using persona-augmented synthetic reviews to capture more complex features, simulating real users who build knowledge of an application across multiple screens before writing a review. ECS achieves 64.1% feature coverage, a 23.8% gain over the state-of-the-art baseline, and covers 72.5% of features in app descriptions, capturing the most prominent features. Our failure analysis shows statelessness and exploration discoverability as main reasons of failures, providing future directions.
item.dc:creator: Ha Min Son, Huan Ren, Huan Song, Zhe Zhao, Xin Liu

item.title: A Multi-Modal Robotic Framework for Physical GUI Interaction Testing
item.description: arXiv:2611.06939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated testing of mobile applications remains challenging when realistic user interactions must be reproduced and GUI behavior verified without relying on invasive mechanisms such as instrumentation or ADB-level control. Existing approaches, including DLD and R-DLD, detect data loss triggered by activity restarts but still depend on system-level access, which limits their applicability on real devices. This doctoral research proposes RFNIT, a multi-modal, fully non-invasive robotic framework for physical GUI interaction testing on smartphones. RFNIT supports end-to-end automation by perceiving the device state through external sensing and executing physical interactions, enabling human-like actions while preserving reproducibility and execution accuracy. The framework integrates a vision-based perception module, an LLM-driven reasoning agent, and a robotic actuator capable of performing touch, swipe, and typing gestures. Multimodal data, including external camera images and OCR-extracted text, are combined to identify GUI elements and guide subsequent testing decisions. Preliminary results indicate that RFNIT accurately recognizes buttons, text fields, and virtual keyboards from external camera input, achieving over 85\% visual detection accuracy. Ongoing and future work will focus on improving robustness, repeatability, and coverage of GUI states during long-running testing sessions.

item.title: Beyond the Agent Harness: Boundary Criteria for Software-Factory Orchestration - A Single-Operator Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.06946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Several recent systems add a layer above the coding-agent harness that organises many agent runs into continuous delivery. The existence of such a layer is not our contribution. What is missing is a rule for deciding which layer a mechanism or a failure belongs to. We propose boundary criteria based on an operational definition of a run. A mechanism confined to one run belongs to the agent harness. One that coordinates runs, hands state from one run to a later one, or is updated from run outcomes belongs to a factory harness. One that must change with the application domain belongs to the domain layer. Two residual tests assign infrastructure and model causes. For failures, we code where the defect originated, which control failed to stop it, and where it was fixed as three separate fields, and we require positive evidence before attributing a failure to the environment. We developed the criteria on documented failures from a single operator's pipeline serving six projects and on 26 components of three published systems. We then froze them and had two model coders of the same family apply them to the same descriptions of 46 held-out units. They agreed on all 26 mechanism layers and on 18-19 of 20 incident fields (kappa 0.86-0.93), but both coders recorded the incident as undetermined or unrecorded in 8-13 of the 20 cases per field, and each flagged half of all units as ambiguous, mostly for missing information. The check exposed conflicts in the rules; a revision that separates mechanism classification from incident attribution resolves them but, in a sensitivity re-coding, agreed less (kappa 0.78-0.93). Agreement here is neither accuracy nor usefulness, and human coders have not yet been tested. Case evidence and seven hypotheses are reported as preliminary.

item.title: How Python Audio Libraries Change Across Releases: Module Structure and Documentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.06947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developers who upgrade a Python audio library need to know what changed in the code they import and whether the release notes say so. Release notes and breaking changes have been mined for general software, but the module structure of audio libraries and its documentation have not been studied together. We mine 56 audio repositories used in machine learning workflows: the import graph of 49 packages at 1,395 releases, joined to 20,864 release-note and changelog entries, labeled by three open-weight language models and checked against two human coders. We find that (1) the set of a package's top-level modules is unchanged in 86.1% of consecutive release pairs, while the set of module files is unchanged in 61.4%. (2) A major increment changes the top level 5.2 times as often as another increment, and major and 0.x minor increments together account for 48.7% of the observed changes. (3) When a release removes modules, its notes name 8.9% of the removal units under a lexical match, an estimated 4.3% after a hand check of the matches. (4) Longer notes are more likely to contain an entry labeled as structural, and within each length band this proportion is also higher for releases with module removals. We intend to release the aligned dataset and the pipeline

item.title: When Does Combining Software-Effort Estimates Help? Evidence from Four Public Project Datasets
item.description: arXiv:2611.06948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Combining estimates can reduce individual prediction errors, but an ensemble may also dilute an unusually accurate estimator or repeat errors shared by its members. We study these competing effects on four archival software-effort datasets (Kitchenham: 145 projects, Desharnais: 77, China: 499, Maxwell: 63) with 100 repeated 70/30 training and test partitions per dataset. Three conventional models (parametric regression, analogy, and random forest) are combined with each other and, in Kitchenham, with a recorded human estimate. Out-of-fold calibration errors drive five combination rules: equal weighting, inverse-MSE weighting, a nonnegative simplex combination, signed Bates-Granger weighting, and Bates-Granger with covariance shrinkage. All preprocessing is learned within training folds. Model-error correlations range from 0.54 to 0.97. In Kitchenham, the human estimate dominates: equal weighting raises mean test log-MAE from 0.239 to 0.455, a loss that remains significant under a corrected resampled t-test with Holm adjustment, whereas the simplex rule limits the increase to 0.250. In Desharnais, China, and Maxwell, every rule lowers mean log-MAE (by 1.3 to 8.6%) and BG with shrinkage beats the calibration-selected individual on 75, 83, and 83 of 100 splits, but none of these gains is statistically distinguishable from zero once the overlap between repeated splits is accounted for. On a completion-year split of Desharnais, equal weighting becomes slightly worse and inverse-MSE is near the individual baseline, while simplex and shrinkage retain mean gains of about 5%. Combining correlated effort estimates is therefore a conditional decision: the harm of naive pooling next to a dominant source is clear, while the benefit elsewhere is small and uncertain.

item.title: KG-AST for Cheaper CI/CD: Budgeted Test Selection and AI Bug Review
item.description: arXiv:2611.06950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous integration and AI-assisted review spend the same budget on every commit, although few commits introduce bugs. We study KG-AST, which scores each commit risk from git history and code-graph features before heavy tests or AI review run, so the budget goes to the riskiest commits first, and which hands the AI reviewer only a graph slice around the change. On 155 open-source projects in 11 languages, a single cross-language model trained on other projects ranks commits so that heavy testing of the riskiest 20% covers 49-64% of bug-introducing commits depending on the language, against 20% for random selection and 40-55% for testing the biggest change first. Every language beats the biggest-change baseline, by 3.8 to 13.2 points. In 20 Java projects the gain at a 20% budget is 15.1 points (64.6% vs 49.5%, 95% interval +11.6 to +18.4), and the model wins in 19 of the 20 projects. About twelve training projects suffice; richer features, tuning and cleaner labels did not help. An AI reviewer that sees only a commit's diff finds 26% of later-fixed defects exactly (32% with graph context), and about half of its findings that did not match a later fix were judged real by independent AI judges. A static call-graph selector runs about 8% of a test suite while including a test written for the fix in 85% of 67 fix commits. The Poincare embedding used in our retrieval work adds nothing measurable here: commit-risk AUC, bug review and severity ranking are unchanged or worse. The labels are noisy and the budget metric assumes a heavy test catches the bug it covers; no CI minutes were measured.

item.title: Operationalizing Responsible AI in MLOps and ML Production: A Systematic Literature Review
item.description: arXiv:2611.06961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled systems are increasingly deployed in operational environments where machine learning (ML) models interact with changing data, users, infrastructure, and organizational processes. While Responsible AI principles are widely discussed, less is known about how these principles are translated into concrete mechanisms within Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) and ML production workflows. This paper reports a systematic literature review of studies that operationalize Responsible AI in ML production. The review synthesizes evidence across monitoring and runtime assurance, audit and compliance, ML lifecycle integration, and traceability/provenance/documentation. Across the final study set, the literature shows a shift from abstract ethical principles toward engineering mechanisms such as drift monitoring, runtime checks, audit logs, provenance records, evidence bundles, governance gates, policy-as-code, model passports, and compliance-oriented documentation. However, the evidence base remains uneven: many studies propose architectures or prototypes, while fewer evaluate the mechanisms in realistic production settings, longitudinal operations, or organizational governance workflows. The review identifies a central gap around integrated, evidence-producing Responsible MLOps: current mechanisms often detect, document, or govern isolated parts of the ML lifecycle, but rarely connect runtime signals, ML lifecycle provenance, human accountability, and compliance evidence into closed operational loops. These findings motivate future software engineering research on traceable, evaluable, and operationally integrated Responsible AI support for ML production.

item.title: When Can Self-Play Fix a False Belief? Answer Keys, Pass Bands and Replacement Rules in an Execution-Grounded Loop
item.description: arXiv:2611.06965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-play loops in which a model writes tasks, derives an answer key and trains on its own matching solutions are often called grounded when the key comes from executing code. We ask which false beliefs such a loop removes. We run expert-iteration self-play with Qwen3-4B-Base on output-prediction tasks, vary the source of the answer key, and track natural beliefs about Python semantics and two misreadings of task specifications planted by fine-tuning ("at most n" read as < n; "the k-th smallest" read as 0-indexed). Executing the generator's own code gave a key that encoded the "at most" misreading on every audited task, and training on it never raised the truth rate above 0.03. A key from an implementation by the unplanted model, a teacher without the error, raised it to 0.23-0.58 after three rounds in four runs. A correct key is not sufficient: the pass band, which keeps tasks solved 1-7 times of 8, admits almost no corrective task while a belief is held on nearly every sample. Execution keys sharply reduced both natural runtime beliefs on diagnostic items in both seeds. Corrections came with replacement rules that fail on neighbouring items the old belief got right. The robust case, present in all four spec runs, is that after the "at most" fix the model increasingly counts the nearest value above a limit that is absent from the list (overcount 0.18-0.38 of control samples at round 3), a case our planted generators almost never wrote (4 of 10,924 tasks); diagnostic-only metrics miss it. Asked for those cases, the planted generator wrote none in 2,061 checkable tasks, against 27% for the untrained unplanted model in one round. Both generators often moved the request into the specification instead ("the cap itself does not count"), and a decorrelated key follows the specification.

item.title: Call-Level Revision Contracts for LLM-Authored Workflows
item.description: arXiv:2611.06967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Durable execution engines replay a recorded history and do not compare activity payloads. When a model repairs a workflow that failed partway through, it must either pay again for calls that succeeded or accept a recorded result whose payload changed. We define a revision contract for workflows whose orchestration code is written by a model. Each capability call carries a structural identity built from its callsite, its fanout position, and its occurrence count, and the identity stays stable under rewrites that leave the call in place, so committed identities form a frozen prefix. The frozen unit is the call expression, and the surrounding code stays writable. A static gate rejects a rewrite that would change a committed call before a container starts. A runtime digest stops a changed payload at a committed identity, and an occurrence ledger names a repeated paid payload. Under three assumptions, a candidate the gate accepts replays every committed call it invokes, executes only new work, and reports the identities it skips. No local identity is both relocation-invariant and free of wrong reuse, so callsite identity turns a relocation into a pre-spend stop. On media workflows, 22 gate-passed repairs replay 258 committed identities with no duplicate, and a live six-way fanout makes seven paid calls instead of twelve. A 12-task customer-support study applies the same identity, replay, and boundary checks on two models.
item.dc:creator: Chenyang Jiang, Benyang Pan, Puqu Wu

item.title: An LLM-Orchestrated Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Verifying Diagnostic Signal Reachability in Electronic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.07040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diagnostic Signal Reachability (DSR) captures whether board-level health signals are observable by management controllers, including baseboard management controllers (BMCs), complex programmable logic devices (CPLDs), and other smart controllers. Verifying DSR is essential for field diagnosability in datacenter fleets, where one design is deployed at massive scale, yet it remains largely manual, since each signal is traced by hand across schematic sheets, renamed nets, series components, and monitoring devices. Large language models (LLMs) are attractive but unreliable at structural connectivity reasoning, where over-claiming can silently hide a rare coverage gap. We present NetFlow-DSR, a neuro-symbolic framework in which an LLM orchestrates the DSR pipeline and resolves device roles mainly from part-name families and library pin names, consulting specifications only for ambiguous parts. Pin directionality is read from the design library, and deterministic graph engines verify connectivity over the authoritative netlist. The pipeline detects diagnostic nets, canonicalizes renamed net fragments, and performs controller-seeded, power-aware breadth-first search over an admissibility graph that credits device-mediated monitoring. Each verdict carries an auditable trace card whose proof path is the witness. Across five production boards from an AI platform, covering 421 expert-graded signals, a three-stage ablation improves pooled F1 from 0.578 to 0.944. Because a monitored verdict is emitted only with a proof path, the verifier is sound by construction, and precision and specificity were 100% in the evaluated data. In a cross-model study on the system-controller module, precision remained 100% across three LLMs while recall tracked each model's device-semantic extraction. Precision therefore depends on the netlist-grounded verifier and correct device semantics rather than on any single LLM.
item.dc:creator: Heba Jaradat, Mohammed-Khalil Ghali, Saurabh Kulkarni, Rohan Kulkarni, Sangwon Yoon

item.title: Automatic Assistance to Reduce Information Overload during Software Issue Report Understanding
item.description: arXiv:2611.07109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern issue tracking systems are used to log an issue and track it from its inception to closure. Issue reports with diverse discussions from stakeholders can be large and verbose, making them challenging to analyze quickly. Our developer interviews revealed that they struggled with the diverse information in issue reports and demanded automated techniques to classify and summarize information. We designed a tool, iSum (issue summarizer), that helps with the automatic classification and summarization of information types discussed in issue reports. The summarizer offers two views: 1. Developer View takes an issue report as input and outputs visualized summaries of information in the report. 2. Manager View takes a suite of all issue reports under a given software project as inputs and shows the prevalence and trends of different information types across the reports. We evaluated iSum through three studies. 1. In an empirical study over two benchmarks, iSum offers, on average, 11-13% higher F1-scores than state-of-the-art baselines to detect information types. 2. We conducted a user study in task-based setup with 30 developers to determine iSum's effectiveness in issue exploration scenarios. Results showed increased productivity and accuracy with iSum compared to manual inspection. 3. We assessed iSum's feasibility for development and management tasks. It proved useful to both developers and project managers for issue comprehension and trend monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Salma Begum Tamanna, Gias Uddin, Junaed Younus Khan, Lan Xia, Longyu Zhang

item.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
item.description: arXiv:2611.07166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at https://multistepswe.com.
item.dc:creator: Xiangkai Zeng, Zheng Liu, Zihao Lin

item.title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.07194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create individual levels. These levels range from the easiest, requiring completing only a single missing lemma, to the hardest, requiring proving the target without any supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. A noisy binary search estimates the highest level that an agent can solve reliably. Applied to six open-source Verus projects, SEVERUS generates 819 quests comprising 10,095 levels. Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet can only reliably solve 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas, instead, using alternative proof decompositions. By systematically varying proof context, SEVERUS provides a foundation for constructing verification benchmarks that can continue to challenge increasingly capable coding agents.
item.dc:creator: \'Alvaro F. Silva, Martim Afonso, Nuno Saavedra, Emily First, Alexandra Mendes, Jo\~ao F. Ferreira

item.title: How Should Agents See Code? Rethinking Code Representations for Agentic Software Engineering
item.description: arXiv:2611.07286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for repository-level software engineering tasks. However, most agents still access repositories through raw files, lexical search, and shell commands, treating code primarily as text. This paper investigates map-based code-representation workflows as a design variable in agentic software engineering, examining how different repository views change agents' retrieval behavior, task success, token use, and latency. In this paper, we study five code-representation workflows: abstract syntax trees, call graphs, module dependencies, documentation-enriched search, and a hybrid workflow that combines them. Each workflow exposes a repository map that the agent can query during a task. We evaluate Claude Code with Haiku 4.5 against a raw-tool baseline on four repository-level tasks: fault localization with LinuxFLBench, repository-level code generation and repair with SWE-bench Pro, test generation with SWT-bench, and security patching with SecBench. The results show that representation workflows are most useful as token-saving tools when localization is the bottleneck, while their success gains narrow when the decisive step is patch or test authoring. On LinuxFLBench, all five workflows improve recall@10 over the baseline (0.757-0.829 vs. 0.717) and reduce token usage by 25-39%. On SWE-bench Pro, resolution remains close to the baseline (44.3-50.6% vs. 49.0%) while token usage drops by 17-26%. On SecBench, Callgraph has the highest patch-resolution rate in this sample (34.3% vs. 28.9%) and uses fewer tokens, but all workflows increase latency. On SWT-bench, Hybrid and Docs have the highest reproducing-test rates in this sample (47.8% and 47.2% vs. 44.7%), but all workflows use more tokens and take longer. Overall, map-based workflows change both what the agent inspects and how much it spends, but their benefits are task-dependent rather than universal.
item.dc:creator: Melika Sepidband, Jiho Shin, Song Wang, Hadi Hemmati

item.title: Take It From Here: Evaluating Coding Agents On Project Takeover
item.description: arXiv:2611.07307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents increasingly collaborate on long-term projects. When taking over a project, they need to recover currently applicable requirements from the interaction history and update them in response to new requests. However, most coding benchmarks do not include long interaction histories, and some evaluations that consider history still do not cover the full process from requirement reconstruction to project delivery. We therefore provide agents with the interaction history, current request, and pre-request project environment, ask them to make the requested changes, and assess takeover performance through delivery tests. Across six model-harness configurations and 37 targets eligible for executable validation, the mean complete-delivery rate under Full History is only 4.95%. We then use requirement atoms to independently diagnose a larger set of takeover targets, examining relevant information identification, pre-request state reconstruction, and current request processing. We further supply correct pre-request or target states to examine the remaining difficulties in requirement processing and project modification. The diagnostics show that none of the six configurations produces fully correct post-request requirement states, and a case illustrates omission of previously recovered constraints during updating. With correct target states supplied, the mean complete-delivery rate is 8.11%, with build and regression pass rates of 96.40% and 90.99%, but target-test success remains 9.01%. These results show difficulties in both forming target requirement states and implementing supplied targets in existing projects. Based on these findings, we introduce ReqMemBench, which combines requirement diagnostics with delivery validation to support systematic evaluation of project takeover.
